newsitem.title: UK: BT dives, can't rule out new MCI deal.
newsitem.headline: BT dives, can't rule out new MCI deal.

text.p: British Telecommunications Plc said on Friday it could not rule out renegotiating a $24 billion merger with MCI after America's second biggest long-distance carrier issued a profit warning.

As BT's share plunged around 10 percent, a BT spokesman said the group was looking at what he described as a "complex situation" after MCI announced late on Thursday that this year's losses due to heavy investments in local markets would be more than twice forecasts.
But the BT spokesman said it was too soon to draw any conclusions about the planned merger.
"At this stage, we are simply looking at the figures and anything beyond that is premature," he added.
Shares in BT dived 44p to 433.5p in heavy trade by 1100 GMT as some analysts scaled back profit forecasts for the British telecom giant.

But most analysts in London -- and some from across the Atlantic who had been awake all night watching developments -- said it was unlikely that BT would renegotiate a deal it had hailed as a great strategic acquisition for the last six months.
"I think any renegotiation...would be a loss of face and more importantly damage confidence in BT's ability to deliver strategic goals," said Andrew Harrington, telecoms analyst at Salomon Brothers.

Another analyst, who declined to be named, noted that MCI was a technology leader which unlike BT had not been focused on shareholder returns. But the analyst agreed that any renegotiation of the merger was unlikely.

"On balance it would be seen as too much of an about-face and I think BT would be up for a lot of criticism if a telecoms company of their stature did not understand the difficulties of local loop (markets)," the analyst said. "One must assume BT invested with their eyes fully open."

MCI said it would forge ahead with the heavy investments it has been making to break into local telephone markets despite its efforts being hampered by what it calls "anti-competitive behaviour" from dominant local rivals. Thus earnings in the second half of 1997 and next year would be below expectations, it said.

But a statement by BT's chief executive Sir Peter Bonfield, backing MCI's calls for the effective opening of the U.S. telecoms markets, reassured some concerns that the strategies of the two firms had parted company.
Bonfield urged a proactive approach to regulation to be adopted throughout the world, especially in the United States "which so often provides the lead for others to follow".

Analyst Harrington said MCI's profit warning reinforced Salomon's view that double-digit growth expectations for Concert, the new BT-MCI merged company, in the next three or four years were far too high.

"The strategy (of investing in local markets) makes a huge amount of sense. BT support it, we support it, (but) the cost is going to be a lot higher and the dilution to BT shareholders is going to be a lot higher than people thought," he said.
Although the next five years were going to be difficult amid a fundamental change in the world-wide telecom business, Harrington says BT's decision to merge with MCI secures its long-term prosperity.

MCI said on Thursday local market losses for this year could reach $800 million, more than twice what it had originally planned. Losses in 1998 in its local business could exceed those of this year, it added.

MCI has so far invested more than $1.0 billion in building fibre-optic-based local telephone networks in more than 21 cities and is committed to offering local service in at least 30 cities by the end of the year.
